text: Almost exclusively found within the UK, specifically Scotland, the iron-barred cages over the graves before you, called mort-safes, aren't intended to keep the dead within their graves, but to keep the living out. By the 18th century, many private anatomy colleges already opened in Scotland. The University of Edinburgh Medical School also opened its doors in 1726, which quickly earned an international reputation for excellence in education. Edinburgh had rapidly become one of Europe's greatest centres of medical learning, and prospective students travelled from across Britain and further beyond to learn anatomy from some of the finest physicians of the age. But this led to a problem. To understand the human body, the students needed human bodies to dissect. However, by law, the only corpses that could be used were those of executed criminals. As the medical schools grew, and the demand for bodies far outstripped the supply available legally, In the 18th and early 19th century, the demand was so high that universities started offering payment to anyone that could provide a corpse of the recently deceased. They won't need us. Then we'll find another trade, won't we? Bodies could sell for up to £10, with the working classes often making less than £1 per month. You can imagine how attractive that high a profit could be to anyone needing some extra coin in their pockets. So before long and sinister trade, resurrection men, or resurrectionists, more commonly known nowadays as grave robbers, would sneak into graveyards under the cover of darkness, and would dig into fresh graves and steal the bodies of the recently buried, selling them to the anatomy schools for tidy profits. Hold the lantern steady. I can't see the headstone. The ground's still soft. Won't take long. Get careful with the lid. Don't mark the wood, or they'll know. Hurry! The smell. Shh! Will the watchman will hear you? Grab the legs! The jewelry! Leave it! The bodies worth more, and they'll hang us for the rings. Move! Curiously, oftentimes the valuables buried with the dead were left behind, for stealing property was considered a serious crime, but stealing a corpse? That was a legal grey area. Christians at the time believed that the body needed to remain intact after death, ready for resurrection on judgment day. The thought of a loved one's grave being disturbed was therefore more than a distressing act of theft. It was a desecration of their faith and chances at an afterlife. Some kept watch over the fresh graves for weeks after the funeral, while those who could afford it paid to have the mort saves locked over the graves, installed by families who wished to take no chances in protecting the remains of their loved ones. Those with even more money would even hire a private guard to stand watch outside the grave until the corpse was rotted beyond use for the medical schools. One of the double mort saves here in Greyfriars was erected by Major M.E. Lindsay to protect the graves of his two daughters, who died in 1837 and 1838. The mort saves were quite effective in protecting the graves, leading bodies to be even harder to come by. Two men plunged this ominous chapter of the city's history even further into darkness. For what does one do when there are no more bodies to steal? They make their own. Come in, come in. Warm yourself by the fire. You're very kind, sir. I have nowhere else to go tonight. You look like you need it. God bless you. There's not many who would open their door to a stranger. In 1828, Irish immigrants William Burke and William Hare murdered 16 vulnerable men and women, usually those who they'd hoped would not be noticed missing, such as the elderly, the sick, and those without family, who stayed or were lured to Hare's lodging house. Another stranger in town? The doctor pays well. No questions asked. Kindness, really? They were suffering. 16 now, or is it 17? To the doctor. He wants more. They sold their victims to Edinburgh's Anatomy School at a high price, as they were always relatively uninjured, freshly deceased, and their organs were intact. Their final victim was an Irish woman called Margaret Dougherty. Before they had the chance to sell her body, two lodgers at Hare's boarding house became suspicious and later discovered her dead motionless body hidden beneath a bed. They alerted the authorities, prompting an investigation into the pair. Though the physical evidence against the pair was minimal, the prosecutors offered Hare immunity were he to testify against. I'll testify. I'll tell you everything. Just let me go. Take your deal, Hare, and pray God forgives you, because Edinburgh won't. Hare immediately accepted, bringing an end to their insidious crimes. This is fair! Lord of it's fair! He's a dead man! What are you trying to say? I'm an innocent man! I'm an innocent man! Kill him! Kill him! For the love of God! It wasn't just me! It wasn't just me! Where is he? Silence in the court! Silence! You are found guilty of murder. You are sentenced to hang by the neck until death. I'm taking him to the subjects table now! I'll remember the name, William Burke! You'll all remember it! Burke was convicted and then sentenced to execution by hanging, which took place in January 1829. In a twist of cruel irony, Burke's remains were publicly dissected before thousands of spectators, a fate he had inflicted on so many of his victims. Over 40,000 attended Burke's dissection. People would take turns and would often take souvenirs with them. Mainly layers of skin peeled directly from his exposed body. They also wanted hair dead, but thanks to his immunity, he eventually managed to flee Edinburgh. Historians believe he changed his name, as there is no record of him shortly after his partner's execution. Today, Burke's remains lay in two different places. His skeleton is exposed at the anatomy section of the University of Edinburgh. To this day, his body still belongs to the University. At the Surgeons' Hall Museum, you can find a leather pocketbook made of Burke's skin, a letter signed in red with his blood, and a model of his real head, molded the day of his execution. You can even see the faint mark of the rope around his neck. This is the Scottish irony. He never let people rest in peace. And now, he rests in pieces. The murders led to the enactment of the Anatomy Act of 1832, which allowed medical schools to obtain bodies through legal means, massively reducing the profits gained from the resurrection trade. To this day, the mort-safes remain, silent witnesses to a time when the dead were not guaranteed a chance to rest in peace.
